name: Solute Potential Calculator
seoDesc: Solute potential is the osmotic component of water potential: dissolved solutes lower it, pulling water in. Free solute potential calculator: enter your value
summary:
Solute potential is the osmotic component of water potential: dissolved solutes lower it, pulling water in. It returns solute potential, solute potential, concentration and equivalent NaCl concentration, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator applies the van 't Hoff relation to give solute potential from concentration and temperature, and compares it with pure water at zero. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Solute Potential
sections.html:
Ψ_s = −i × C × R × T

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
inumber of particles the solute dissociates into—
Cconcentrationmol/L
Rgas constant, 8.314J/mol/K
Tabsolute temperatureK

sections.title: How do I use the Solute Potential?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: solute concentration of 0.2 mol/L, temperature of 25°C, ionisation factor (i) of 1.

Substituting them into the formula gives solute potential of -4.96e-04 MPa, solute potential of -0.005 bar, concentration of 200 mmol/L, equivalent nacl concentration of 200 mmol/L.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
0 MPaPure waterthe maximum water potential
−0.1 to −0.5 MPaTypical plant cellmost mesophytes at full turgor
−1 to −2 MPaStressed or salinegrowth slows and stomata close
below −2 MPaSeverehalophytes only; most crops die

  • Solute potential is always negative or zero: solutes can only lower water potential, never raise it.

  • The ionisation factor doubles the effect of sodium chloride, which is why seawater at about 1 mol/L NaCl gives roughly −4.5 MPa.

  • Water potential also has a pressure component, so a turgid cell's total potential can be near zero even though its solute potential is strongly negative.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Forgetting i for a salt, which halves the apparent osmotic effect.
  • Using degrees Celsius in the gas constant term.
  • Reporting solute potential as positive because only the magnitude was calculated.

faq.a: Because pure water at atmospheric pressure is defined as zero, and solutes always reduce the free energy of water.

faq.q: What is the solute potential of 0.1 M sucrose at 20 °C?
What does the Solute Potential actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns solute potential, solute potential, concentration and equivalent NaCl concentration. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
